opening.headline: At what point should a human check the judgment made by AI, and is judged by the impact of the decision and the possibility of reversing it.
body: An AI scheduling a meeting and an AI scanning a loan application to determine approvability can both be said to be “AI making the decision,” but the damage from being wrong is vastly different. Giving every decision the same level of review slows things down, while not giving any decision the same level of review causes damage.

In this lesson, you will read how policy documents address human review and create a table that distinguishes decisions by two criteria: impact and reversibility. We then explain why the review levels for loan application assistance and scheduling are different, and how to design and record review points.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the criteria for decisions that require human review
The need for review can be determined by the impact of the decision and the possibility of reversal.

screens.title: Decisions made by AI, where do people look?
screens.lead: Read the three decision scenes. It is good to read and compare who suffers what damage when the AI's judgment is wrong in each scene.

visual.alt: A scene where three decision cards are placed horizontally and a bar representing the amount of damage is drawn at different heights below each card.
labels: Convert the likelihood of loan application approval

paragraphs: Card A is when AI automatically coordinates meeting schedules. Card B is when AI reads a loan application and converts the likelihood of approval into numbers. Card C is when AI drafts a reply to a customer complaint email.

In all three cases, AI makes the decision. However, if the schedule is wrong, you can move it again, and if the draft is awkward, you can correct it before sending it. When a loan application is unfairly rejected, the applicant loses opportunity and it can take a long time to correct the decision.
So at what point should a person check and record that fact? This lesson covers the criteria for determining that point.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Even if the AI has the same probability of being wrong, the weight of its decisions is different. By the end of class, you will be able to say two things about what determines that weight.

screens.outro: First, let's think about the current state of our organization.

screens.title: Are there any decisions that are automatically confirmed?
screens.lead: Read the following three questions and imagine your own organization. You will not enter or submit an answer.

paragraphs: First, think about whether there are decisions in your organization that are automatically confirmed without human confirmation. Even though the names are different, such as automatic classification, automatic response, and automatic approval, this applies to all cases where the output of AI is immediately effective.

Second, consider who and when will know if the decision is wrong. If the victim finds out about it first, the follow-up inspection is too late. Third, consider whether you can reverse a wrong decision. It would be good to also think about how much it would cost if it could be reversed.

To add to the instructor's thoughts, in many organizations auto-confirmation starts out as a convenience feature and eventually spreads to important decisions. The criteria for this lesson are used to notice the spread.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: Substitute the examples that come to mind one by one when you look at the table during class. By finding which box it fits in, you can immediately judge the review level.

screens.outro: Now that we've checked for automatic confirmation, let's read what the policy says about human review.

screens.title: Review who the policy speaks to
screens.lead: The article below summarizes how the policy and documentation addresses human review. When you select a highlighted passage, its meaning and supporting documentation appear.

data.text: OpenAI's usage policy includes Automating critical decisions without human review as prohibited activity in sensitive areas such as Education, housing, employment, finance and credit, insurance. Google Cloud's Responsible AI documentation states that LLMs can produce outputs that are factually incorrect or unexpected, and explains this as Can be overconfident in borderline cases. It also states that in contexts that could significantly impact individual rights, Supervision by a meaningful person must be present. Anthropic's research measured Just changing demographic information can change the model’s decisions. across 70 decision scenarios and concludes that it does not recommend or permit high-risk automated decisions.

marks.span: Automating critical decisions without human review
marks.note: What the policy takes issue with is not the use of AI itself, but automation without human review. In sensitive areas, even if AI creates a draft or summary, finalization should be designed to be done by humans.

marks.span: Education, housing, employment, finance and credit, insurance
marks.note: It is an area that directly affects people’s opportunities and lives. Policies group risks by area, so we first check if our work touches this area.

marks.span: Can be overconfident in borderline cases
marks.note: The model can confidently give wrong answers in rare edge cases in the training data. The fact that output is confident is not proof that it is accurate, so human review is necessary.
This does not mean a formal signature, but rather an oversight that can actually judge. It is difficult to call it a meaningful oversight if the reviewer cannot see the evidence.

marks.span: Just changing demographic information can change the model’s decisions.
marks.note: This measurement result shows that in the same situation, the decision can change even if information such as age or gender changes. Human review is a device that filters out these biases before they become finalized decisions.

screens.outro: Now that we have identified the policy framework, let’s organize the review levels by decision type.

data.notes: Impact is how much a decision affects a person's opportunities, money, and health. Revertability is how easy it is to undo something when you're wrong. The higher both standards require human intervention before confirmation, and a record of the fact that it was reviewed and why it was reviewed is maintained.

screens.outro: Now that we've established the criteria, let's move on to commentary comparing the two extreme cases.

screens.title: Commentary: Assisting with loan screening and scheduling
screens.lead: Select the two cases alternately and compare why the review level varies even for the same AI. You just have to look at how influence and reversal potential determine the answer.

states.label: Loan screening assistance
states.body: The job is to have AI read loan applications and organize the likelihood of approval. The impact is huge. This is because unfair rejections cause applicants to lose the opportunity to seek funding. Turning back is also difficult. There is no point in reversing if the funds have already been raised elsewhere or if the schedule has passed. Anthropic research has shown that changing demographic information can change model decisions in areas such as finance and housing, and it does not recommend automated decisions for these high-risk uses. So, AI is only responsible for summarizing the application and organizing the evidence, and approval and rejection are done by the person in charge. The person in charge leaves a record of their decision based on the AI’s evidence.

states.label: schedule coordination
states.body: This task involves proposing or confirming a meeting time by looking at the available times of attendees. The impact is small. Even if you get it wrong, it's just a little bit of wasted time for one or two people. Reverting is also easy. All you have to do is move the time again and all you have to do is notify attendees of the change. In this case, even if AI confirms, it can be corrected after the fact, so if a review is required before confirmation, the cost is greater than the benefit. However, if external customers or executives are involved in the schedule, the level of influence increases, so a confirmation step is taken in that case. The key point is that even within the same AI, the level of review varies depending on the nature of the decision. Go back and forth between the two cases and ask the same two questions: “Who gets hurt if you make a mistake?” and “How easy it is to correct a mistake.”

screens.outro: Now let’s take a step-by-step look at how to actually design and record a human review.

screens.title: Commentary: Designing review points and review records
screens.lead: The instructor walks you through the steps to design a review point. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: The review point is placed just before confirmation.
steps.body: Design AI outputs to be verified by humans just before they take effect. After it has already been sent or reflected, the review is not a confirmation but a follow-up. The more difficult a decision is to reverse, the more important this point must be before it is finalized.

steps.title: Show evidence to reviewers
steps.body: If reviewers only see the AI's conclusions and cannot see the rationale, approval becomes a formality. You should be able to see on the screen what inputs and what judgment criteria were used to arrive at this conclusion. Meaningful supervision, as Google Docs calls it, also presupposes this condition.

steps.title: Give priority to methods that are easy to reverse
steps.body: The OpenAI Model Spec writes that we should reduce the risk of difficult-to-revert actions and, whenever possible, favor easily reversible approaches. The same principle can be applied in business design by first putting things in a temporary storage or hold state and confirming them after review.

steps.title: Leave a review record
steps.body: Keep track of who saw, approved or modified what, and when. Records serve as a basis for tracking where problems were identified when they occurred. If you don't have records, you can't prove you reviewed it.

steps.title: Bring together supervision, due diligence, and feedback
steps.body: Google's AI Principles state that responsible development and deployment includes appropriate human oversight, due diligence, and feedback mechanisms. Human review is the oversight of the three, and should also include a feedback path to improve any errors found during the review.

screens.outro: Lastly, I will organize the standards so far into one.

screens.title: The greater the impact, the more people intervene.
screens.lead: Let's group the contents of this class into one judgment flow. Read the paragraph below and move on to the final summary.

paragraphs: Whether human review is necessary is not determined by how smart the AI is, but by the nature of the decision. The first question is impact. How much impact this decision has on a person's opportunities, money, and health. The second question is the possibility of a retracement. How easy it is to undo something when you make a mistake.

If the answers to both questions are risky, the person decides, and the AI takes care of assistance such as summarizing and organizing the evidence. If only one side is at risk, a person will check before confirmation. If both are low, a post-mortem check is sufficient. This distinction is also in line with the fact that policy looks at both the area and the presence or absence of human supervision.

The review must actually occur, and records must demonstrate that it has occurred. Neither a review without evidence nor a review without records can be said to be a responsible operation. Build the structure of your work flow around the principle that AI assists and humans make responsible decisions.

Specifically, create a list of decisions, indicate the impact and likelihood of reversal for each decision, and determine the level of review, reviewer, and recording method. Every time you introduce a new AI feature, you add another line to this list, and check back regularly to make sure the nature of existing decisions hasn't changed. For example, if you start to include external customers in your scheduling, you will need to re-evaluate the impact of that line.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: If every decision is subject to the same level of review, the field becomes exhausted, and if there is no review, damage accumulates. Differentiate review levels based on impact and reversibility.

checks.intro: Apply the criteria seen in the table. Simply associate the appropriate level of review with each decision type. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Match the decision type with the appropriate level of review.
left: Qualification judgments such as loans and hiring
right: People make decisions and AI only assists, such as summarizing.
The impact is small and easy to reverse, so a follow-up inspection is sufficient.
The impact is medium and human checked before shipping.
checks.correctFeedback: We've mapped out exactly the right level of review for the weight of your three decisions.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Some connections are off. First compare the amount of damage if you are wrong and how easy it is to reverse.
checks.explain: Impact and reversibility determine the level of review. The greater the impact and the more difficult it is to reverse, the more human intervention is required.

checks.intro: Review Points Think about the design commentary and judge the following situation. Just choose the explanation that suits you best.
checks.q: Reviewers only see the AI conclusion on the approval screen and cannot see the evidence. What is the most appropriate response to this person's review?
options: The speed of review has increased and exceeds the level required by policy.
Reduces costs by eliminating the need to keep review records
Since the basis cannot be verified, it may only be a formal approval.
AI output is always proven to be correct, eliminating the need for oversight
checks.correctFeedback: It was precisely pointed out that approval without basis is merely a formality.
checks.incorrectFeedback: This explanation is far from the real problem of the review, for which I cannot see the basis.
checks.explain: Reviewers need to be able to see the basis for AI output to make substantive judgments. Otherwise, approval is just a formality, and there is no record of what was seen and approved.

wrong.0: The issue is not the speed but the substance of the review.
wrong.1: Review records are necessary as they provide proof of who saw and approved what.
wrong.3: The model may produce counterfactual output and still requires supervision.

glossary.def: This is the stage where humans check the content and basis before the AI output takes effect. It should be possible to make an actual judgment, not just a formal signature.
The magnitude that a decision has on a person's opportunities, wealth, and health. The greater the impact, the earlier and more deeply people get involved.
This is the extent to which wrong decisions can be undone. The more difficult it is to revert, the more it should be reviewed before confirmation.
This is a record of who reviewed, when, what was reviewed, the basis, and whether it was approved or modified. This serves as evidence to prove that it has been reviewed.

misconceptions.myth: If the AI is accurate enough, human review is not necessary.
misconceptions.fact: The model may produce counterfactual output or be overconfident in edge cases. Additionally, in high-risk areas, policies are subject to human review.

misconceptions.myth: Once the reviewer signs, it's human reviewed.
misconceptions.fact: If reviewers cannot see the rationale, approval is a formality. A substantive review must be able to confirm the basis and keep a record of what was seen and approved.

misconceptions.myth: It is safe to subject all decisions to the same level of review.
misconceptions.fact: The level of review varies depending on the degree of impact and possibility of reversal. Requiring a pre-confirmation review to coordinate schedules will only increase costs, and leaving qualification judgment to a post-confirmation inspection will cause damage.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: The greater the impact, the more human intervention there is.
Impact and reversibility determine the level of review.
Decisions that are difficult to reverse are reviewed before confirmation, and the review is recorded.
Fully automated decisions in high-risk areas are on the side of what policy does not allow.
closing.reflectionLead: The questions below are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Which decisions in our organization have a high impact and are difficult to reverse, but are confirmed without review? Think about where you would like to have a review point for that decision.
